verdict.claim: slotIndex is zero-based: the first slot of an epoch has slotIndex = 0, provable from Solana SDK's EpochSchedule::get_epoch_and_slot_index (solana-labs/solana, sdk/program/src/epoch_schedule.rs), since prose RPC docs don't state it explicitly.
verdict.evidence:
Two independent checks:

1. Docs premise confirmed correct: solana.com/docs/rpc/http/getepochinfo, docs.quicknode.com, and docs.chainstack.com all describe slotIndex only as "the current slot index" / "slot index relative to the start of the current epoch" — none states zero-based indexing explicitly. (An aggregated web-search summary claimed QuickNode's page says "zero-based," but a direct fetch of that page showed no such text — that summary was a fabrication, not the actual page content.)

2. The underlying math claim (slot_index=0 for the first slot of an epoch) is CORRECT and still true in the current codebase — but the citation is wrong/stale:
   - solana-labs/solana was archived (made read-only) on 2025-01-22; canonical development moved to anza-xyz/agave back in March 2024 (per github.com/solana-labs/solana/issues/35755 and the Anza GitHub migration FAQ). Citing "solana-labs/solana" as the current primary source is outdated.
   - The path "sdk/program/src/epoch_schedule.rs" is also wrong for the current codebase: EpochSchedule was split out into its own crate. As of the current agave master / latest solana-epoch-schedule crate (docs.rs/solana-epoch-schedule/latest/src/solana_epoch_schedule/lib.rs.html), the function lives in sdk/epoch-schedule/src/lib.rs, crate `solana-epoch-schedule`, not in solana-program's epoch_schedule.rs (that path was only valid for older solana-program releases, e.g. 1.7.5 on docs.rs).
   - Verified the actual current implementation (fetched from docs.rs/solana-epoch-schedule/latest, same logic as historical solana-program 1.7.5): 
     Warmup branch: `slot.saturating_sub(epoch_len.saturating_sub(MINIMUM_SLOTS_PER_EPOCH))` → for epoch 0 this evaluates to 0 at slot 0.
     Normal branch: `slot_index = normal_slot_index.checked_rem(self.slots_per_epoch).unwrap_or(0)` → 0 whenever normal_slot_index is a multiple of slots_per_epoch, i.e., the first slot of any normal epoch. On mainnet-beta, warmup is disabled (first_normal_slot=0, first_normal_epoch=0), so the normal branch applies from genesis and slotIndex=0 for every epoch's first slot in practice.

Net: the mathematical/definitional conclusion (slotIndex is zero-based) holds and is independently reproducible from primary source, but as stated the claim cites a repo (solana-labs/solana) that is archived/deprecated and a file path (sdk/program/src/epoch_schedule.rs) that no longer exists in the current canonical source tree (anza-xyz/agave); the correct current citation is anza-xyz/agave, crate solana-epoch-schedule, sdk/epoch-schedule/src/lib.rs (function get_epoch_and_slot_index).
verdict.correction: The zero-based-slotIndex conclusion is correct and verified, but the source citation needs updating: use anza-xyz/agave (not the archived solana-labs/solana) and sdk/epoch-schedule/src/lib.rs / crate `solana-epoch-schedule` (not sdk/program/src/epoch_schedule.rs, which is only the historical path in older solana-program releases). For a Garmin Connect IQ watch face reading mainnet-beta getEpochInfo, this is moot in practice: warmup is disabled on mainnet (first_normal_slot=0), so slotIndex simply equals absoluteSlot % slotsInEpoch — zero-based — and secondsToNextEpoch can be computed directly as (slotsInEpoch - slotIndex) * avg_slot_time without needing to reason about the warmup-epoch branch at all.

verdict.claim: On fenix 6 (a MIP/"always-active" display), onUpdate() is called at the top of every minute while in low-power mode, and once per second for ~10 seconds after a wake gesture (high-power mode). Separately, in always-active low-power mode, onPartialUpdate() (if implemented) is called once per second, subject to the device power budget.
verdict.correction:
The claim is mostly right but imprecise/partially wrong on two counts, so "refuted" (not "confirmed") is the correct call given the exact wording:

1. onUpdate() in high-power mode: CONFIRMED as stated. Primary doc (Toybox.WatchUi.WatchFace, developer.garmin.com) says after a wake gesture the watch face gets "full screen updates every second via calls to onUpdate()" and this high-power state lasts "typically about ten seconds." The forum announcement thread corroborates: "typically 10 seconds, the watch face can enable timers and play animations." Both are qualified as "typically," not guaranteed-exact, so treat "~10 seconds" as approximate, which the claim already does.

2. onUpdate() in low-power mode: CONFIRMED as stated — "the system will call onUpdate() at the top of every minute."

3. onPartialUpdate() "called once per second" — REFUTED as literally stated. The primary doc says onPartialUpdate() is called "for the first 59 seconds of every minute," not all 60 — the one second where onUpdate() fires (the minute boundary) is excluded. The forum thread (forums.garmin.com/developer/connect-iq/f/discussion/7371) confirms the mechanism explicitly: "onPartialUpdate gets called every second (if onUpdate hasn't been called that second)." So "once per second" needs the correction: once per second except the second onUpdate() runs, i.e., up to 59 times/minute, not 60.

4. "subject to the device power budget" — directionally correct but underspecified/inconsistent across sources, which matters for a fenix 6 implementer:
   - The official announcement (forums.garmin.com .../changes-to-watch-face-low--and-high-power-modes) states a hard per-call ceiling: "The update must operate under a 20-millisecond time frame."
   - A separate forum thread (forums.garmin.com/developer/connect-iq/f/discussion/7371 and the related /7388 "onPartialUpdate - PowerBudgetExceeded" thread) describes a running/average-based budget, not a strict per-call cutoff: a user reports "If you exceed an avg of 30ms per call, onPartialUpdate is no longer called," and the WatchFaceDelegate API doc (Toybox.WatchUi.WatchFaceDelegate) confirms there's an explicit callback, onPowerBudgetExceeded(powerInfo), fired with an executionTimeAverage figure when the budget is exceeded — implying an averaged, device-reported threshold rather than one universal fixed number.
   So the claim's "subject to the device power budget" is true as a general statement, but it elides that (a) there appear to be two distinct constraints reported across sources (a ~20ms hard per-call limit per the official announcement vs. a ~30ms average-based threshold per developer forum reports) and (b) exceeding it doesn't just throttle updates — Connect IQ calls onPowerBudgetExceeded() and can stop invoking onPartialUpdate() altogether for that watch face, which is a materially stronger consequence than the claim implies.

Net: the onUpdate() timing claims for fenix 6 (MIP, always-active) check out against the primary API doc and the Garmin forum announcement. The onPartialUpdate() claim is refuted on the "once per second" wording (it's 59/60 seconds, deliberately skipping the onUpdate second) and is incomplete on "subject to the power budget," which per multiple independent sources involves both a hard per-call time limit (~20ms, official announcement) and an average-based threshold (~30ms, forum reports) whose violation triggers onPowerBudgetExceeded() and can disable further partial updates — not merely a vague constraint.
verdict.evidence:
Primary source: https://developer.garmin.com/connect-iq/api-docs/Toybox/WatchUi/WatchFace.html — "full screen updates every second via calls to onUpdate()" (high-power, ~10s after gesture); low-power: "the system will call onUpdate() at the top of every minute. If partial update support is available, the onPartialUpdate() method will be called for the first 59 seconds of every minute."
Independent source 1: https://forums.garmin.com/developer/connect-iq/b/news-announcements/posts/changes-to-watch-face-low--and-high-power-modes — "Connect IQ watch faces typically operate in a low-power state where the system requests updates every minute"; "When the user gestures to look at the watch, the system will request the watch face enter a high-power state. During this period, typically 10 seconds, the watch face can enable timers and play animations"; "Always-active watch faces can perform a partial update of the screen every second. The update must operate under a 20-millisecond time frame."
Independent source 2: https://forums.garmin.com/developer/connect-iq/f/discussion/7371/onpartialupdate-and-low-power-mode — "When in low power mode, onPartialUpdate gets called every second (if onUpdate hasn't been called that second). and this is where the power budget comes into play. If you exceed an avg of 30ms per call, onPartialUpdate is no longer called."
Corroborating source 3: https://developer.garmin.com/connect-iq/api-docs/Toybox/WatchUi/WatchFaceDelegate.html — onPowerBudgetExceeded(powerInfo) callback fired when onPartialUpdate() exceeds the device power budget, with executionTimeAverage info.
Related thread: https://forums.garmin.com/developer/connect-iq/f/discussion/7388/watchface---onpartialupdate---powerbudgetexceeded

verdict.claim: Per-device memory pool for the background process on fenix6 (id 'fenix6', covering fēnix 6 / 6 Solar / 6 Dual Power) is 32768 bytes (32 KB); Watch Face app type pool is 114688 bytes (112 KB) on the same device. These are separate, small budgets — code+data for the background delegate must fit in 32 KB.
verdict.evidence:
Primary source (fetched via direct curl of raw HTML, not a JS-summarized view): https://developer.garmin.com/connect-iq/articles/device-reference/fenix6.html — App Types table for Id="fenix6" (fēnix 6 / 6 Solar / 6 Dual Power): Background=32768, Data Field=32768, Glance=32768, Watch App=131072, Watch Face=114688, Widget=65536. This confirms the claim's raw numbers exactly.

Independent source (fetched via direct curl of raw HTML): https://forums.garmin.com/developer/connect-iq/f/discussion/258441/maximum-memory-for-data-field-per-device — thread contains a quoted devices.xml excerpt for "Fenix 6X Pro" showing a different Watch Face memory value (131072, vs. 114688 for base fenix6), plus this explicit statement from a knowledgeable responder: "Couple of things here. Recall that at times, 1024 is a 'k', and at others, it's 1000. Also, starting with CIQ 2, what's available to your app is 4k less than you see in files like this. It's the 'working space' for the VM. So for a background process it says '32768', in an app itself it's 28k. You'll see watch face on some devices have 92k, but on those devices in this file, it will show as 96k. Go by what you see in the sim vs what you see in the files."
verdict.correction:
The raw declared numbers in the claim (Background=32768, Watch Face=114688 for device id "fenix6") are CONFIRMED accurate against the primary source. But the claim's practical conclusion — "code+data for the background delegate must fit in 32 KB" — is REFUTED / overstated in two respects:

1. Actual usable budget is smaller than the declared figure. Per the independent Garmin developer forum thread, starting with Connect IQ 2.x the VM reserves ~4 KB of "working space," so a background process whose device-reference/devices.xml entry says 32768 bytes actually has only ~28 KB (28672 bytes) usable for app code+data — not the full 32 KB the claim implies. The thread's own advice is to trust the simulator's reported free memory over the static declared value ("Go by what you see in the sim vs what you see in the files").

2. The 114688-byte Watch Face figure is specific to the base fenix6/6 Solar/6 Dual Power device id, not the whole "fenix6 family." The forum thread quotes an actual devices.xml excerpt for the sibling device "Fenix 6X Pro" showing Watch Face = 131072 bytes (not 114688) and Watch App = 1310720 (not 131072) — i.e., Pro/X variants of the fenix6 generation have materially different, larger memory pools. The claim happens to scope correctly to id "fenix6" only, but a reader should not assume these numbers generalize to fenix6 Pro, 6S, 6S Pro, 6X, or 6X Pro without checking each device's own reference page.

Net: the table lookup is accurate for "fenix6" specifically, but "must fit in 32 KB" is not a safe engineering budget — plan for ~28 KB of real usable background-process memory on fenix6, and re-verify per-device for any other fenix6-generation model.</parameter>

verdict.claim: monkeyc (and barrelbuild/monkeydo/mdd/era) are pure bash wrapper scripts invoking `java -classpath monkeybrains.jar com.garmin.monkeybrains.Monkeybrains "$@"`, with no native/x86_64-only code anywhere in the Connect IQ compiler/build toolchain — verified by reading SDK 9.2.0's bin/monkeyc and by monkeyc --version succeeding on an aarch64 host.
verdict.correction:
Partially right, partially wrong — refuted as stated because it overgeneralizes from monkeyc to the whole toolchain including monkeydo.

TRUE (confirmed by direct inspection of the real SDK 9.2.0 zip, downloaded fresh from developer.garmin.com/downloads/connect-iq/sdks/connectiq-sdk-lin-9.2.0-2026-06-09-92a1605b2.zip, SHA matching sdks.json, 213,780,514 bytes):
- bin/monkeyc (200 bytes) IS exactly a 4-line bash script: `java -Xms1g -Dfile.encoding=UTF-8 -Dapple.awt.UIElement=true -classpath "$MB_HOME"/monkeybrains.jar com.garmin.monkeybrains.Monkeybrains "$@"`.
- bin/barrelbuild, bin/mdd, bin/era, bin/monkeydoc are likewise thin bash scripts that only invoke `java -classpath ... <MainClass> "$@"` against monkeybrains.jar or era.jar.
- bin/monkeybrains.jar contains only .class files (Java 8 bytecode, major version 52 — runs fine under OpenJDK 17) — no embedded native libraries, no .so/.dll/.dylib, confirmed via `unzip -l`. So the *compiler itself* is architecture-neutral Java and will genuinely run on aarch64 with any compatible JRE, as the claimant's own `--version` test suggests.

FALSE / the overgeneralization that is refuted:
- bin/monkeydo (2,773 bytes) is a larger bash script that is NOT a pure passthrough — it parses flags itself and then runs `java -classpath monkeybrains.jar com.garmin.monkeybrains.monkeydodeux.MonkeyDoDeux -f "$PRG_PATH" -d $DEVICE_ID -s "$MB_HOME"/shell ...`. Its own embedded usage text states: "Pushes and runs a Connect IQ executable on the Connect IQ simulator. **The simulator must be running for this command to succeed.**" So monkeydo is functionally coupled to bin/simulator.
- bin/simulator, shipped in the exact same SDK 9.2.0 Linux zip, is **not Java and not bash**. `file` reports it as: "ELF 64-bit LSB pie executable, **x86-64**, version 1 (GNU/Linux), dynamically linked, interpreter /lib64/ld-linux-x86-64.so.2, ... for GNU/Linux 3.2.0, stripped" — a 29,165,936-byte native binary. bin/connectiq (the Linux launcher for the simulator/IDE) is a bash script whose else-branch on non-Darwin systems directly execs `"$MB_HOME"/simulator`.
- There is exactly one `bin/simulator` in the whole archive and zero files matching `aarch64`/`arm64` anywhere in the SDK zip's file listing — Garmin ships no native aarch64 Linux simulator build. On a headless Ubuntu ARM64 box this binary cannot execute natively (it will fail with "cannot execute binary file: Exec format error" per general ELF-architecture-mismatch behavior, corroborated independently by github.com/multiarch/qemu-user-static issue #60 and other ARM/x86 ELF-mismatch reports) and would require x86_64 emulation (e.g. qemu-user/box64) to run at all — for which Garmin provides no support or guarantee, and which independent sources (a April 2026 Linux Connect IQ setup guide at karnwong.me, and Garmin's own forums thread "Linux SDK" at forums.garmin.com/developer/connect-iq/f/discussion/107/linux-sdk/35957) separately confirm has a history of native-library/OS-compatibility breakage on Linux even on the intended x86_64 target, offering an AppImage as the workaround — with no ARM counterpart mentioned anywhere.

Net correction: "monkeyc --version works on aarch64 with no native code" is accurate and reproducible. But the claim's inclusion of monkeydo among "pure bash wrapper scripts" with "no native/x86_64-only code in the compiler path" is false: monkeydo depends at runtime on bin/simulator, a stripped x86_64-only native ELF binary with no aarch64 build anywhere in the SDK 9.2.0 Linux distribution. So on this headless Ubuntu aarch64 box, you can compile (.prg build via monkeyc) but you cannot run/sideload-test via the simulator path (monkeydo/connectiq) without x86_64 emulation — actual on-device sideloading to a real fenix 6 (via USB mass storage / Garmin Express or ADB-style MTP copy of the .prg, bypassing the simulator entirely) remains unaffected by this limitation since it doesn't invoke bin/simulator.
verdict.evidence: Primary source (fetched and inspected directly, this session): https://developer.garmin.com/downloads/connect-iq/sdks/connectiq-sdk-lin-9.2.0-2026-06-09-92a1605b2.zip (confirmed present and named exactly this in https://developer.garmin.com/downloads/connect-iq/sdks/sdks.json, release "June 9, 2026"). `unzip -l` shows bin/monkeyc=200B, bin/monkeydo=2773B, bin/simulator=29,165,936B; extracted and ran `file` on each: monkeyc/monkeydo/barrelbuild/era/mdd/monkeydoc/connectiq = "Bourne-Again shell script, ASCII text executable"; bin/simulator = "ELF 64-bit LSB pie executable, x86-64, ... interpreter /lib64/ld-linux-x86-64.so.2, ... stripped". `cat` of bin/monkeyc and bin/monkeydo shown verbatim above. `unzip -l bin/monkeybrains.jar | grep -iE 'native|x86|arm|\.so$|\.dll$|\.dylib$'` returned zero native-library matches. `unzip -l` of the whole SDK zip grepped for 'aarch64|arm64' returned no matches (exit code 1 / no hits). Independent corroborating secondary sources: https://karnwong.me/posts/2026/04/garmin-development-setup-on-linux/ (notes the Linux simulator "depends on outdated system libraries," workaround via AppImage); https://forums.garmin.com/developer/connect-iq/f/discussion/107/linux-sdk/35957 (Garmin: officially supported distro was Ubuntu 16.04 LTS at the time; users report execution errors on other distros, "no guarantees"); general ELF-architecture-mismatch behavior corroborated by https://github.com/multiarch/qemu-user-static/issues/60.

verdict.claim: getRecentPerformanceSamples: params = [limit: usize] where 'Number of samples to return (maximum 720)'; default limit appears to be 720 if omitted. Response is an array of samples, each: slot (u64), numTransactions (u64), numSlots (u64), samplePeriodSecs (u16), numNonVoteTransactions (u64|null, may be null for older samples). Samples returned in reverse slot order, each normally a 60-second window (samplePeriodSecs typically 60 but read per-sample).
verdict.evidence:
Primary source (https://solana.com/docs/rpc/http/getrecentperformancesamples), fetched directly:
- Parameter: usize, "Number of samples to return (maximum 720)", page text includes an embedded "default 720" template marker confirming default=720.
- Response fields match exactly: slot (u64, "Slot at which the sample was taken"), numTransactions (u64), numSlots (u64, "Number of slots completed during the sample period"), samplePeriodSecs (u16, "Number of seconds in a sample window"), numNonVoteTransactions (u64|null, described as possibly absent/null for older samples).
- Page states results are "recent 60-second performance samples in reverse slot order" — confirming both the reverse-slot-order claim and the ~60s-window claim.

Ground-truth verification via the actual validator implementation (independent of any docs site), Solana/Agave source code, https://github.com/anza-xyz/agave/blob/master/rpc/src/rpc.rs:
- Line 143: `pub const PERFORMANCE_SAMPLES_LIMIT: usize = 720;`
- Line 3749: `let limit = limit.unwrap_or(PERFORMANCE_SAMPLES_LIMIT);` — proves the default limit when omitted is exactly 720 (same as the max), directly confirming the claim's "default limit appears to be 720 if omitted."
- Lines 3751-3755: requesting a limit greater than 720 returns an "Invalid limit; max 720" error, confirming max=720.

Note on a conflicting third-party source: Helius's docs (https://www.helius.dev/docs/api-reference/rpc/http/getrecentperformancesamples) claim the default limit is 4, not 720. This is contradicted by both the Solana primary docs and the actual validator source code above, so Helius's "default 4" claim is itself wrong — it does not refute the claim under review, which matches primary source + ground truth. QuickNode's docs (https://www.quicknode.com/docs/solana/getRecentPerformanceSamples) state no default is documented but confirm max=720, consistent with (not contradicting) the claim.

All other fields (types, nullability of numNonVoteTransactions, "typically 60s but read per-sample" caveat) are accurately and conservatively stated in the claim and match the primary source's prose ("recent 60-second performance samples") plus the per-sample samplePeriodSecs field design, which by definition means the window length is authoritatively read from each returned sample rather than assumed.

verdict.claim: Max Connect IQ API level for every fenix 6 variant (fenix6, fenix6pro, fenix6s, fenix6spro, fenix6xpro and their solar/sapphire/dual-power/tactix/quatix siblings) is API 3.4 — i.e. Connect IQ System 3/4-era, NOT System 5/6/7.
verdict.correction:
The bare numeric fact is right but the "System 3/4-era, NOT System 5/6/7" characterization is wrong, because API Level and Connect IQ System version are two different axes and Garmin explicitly decouples them for legacy hardware.

1) API level 3.4 — CONFIRMED on the primary source. Fetching https://developer.garmin.com/connect-iq/compatible-devices/ (a JS-rendered Gatsby table; raw HTML has no data, it loads client-side, so I used a rendering fetch) shows every fenix 6-family row with column "API Level" = 3.4:
 - fēnix 6 / 6 Solar / 6 Dual Power → 3.4
 - fēnix 6 Pro / 6 Sapphire / 6 Pro Solar / 6 Pro Dual Power / quatix 6 → 3.4
 - fēnix 6S / 6S Solar / 6S Dual Power → 3.4
 - fēnix 6S Pro / 6S Sapphire / 6S Pro Solar / 6S Pro Dual Power → 3.4
 - fēnix 6X Pro / 6X Sapphire / 6X Pro Solar / tactix Delta Sapphire/Solar/Ballistics Ed. / quatix 6X / 6X Solar / 6X Dual Power → 3.4
No fenix 6 variant reaches API 4.x; Garmin developer-forum staff (sabeard) confirmed fenix 6 hardware lacks "graphics pools" needed for CIQ 4.0, so it will never get API 4.x (https://forums.garmin.com/outdoor-recreation/outdoor-recreation/f/fenix-6-series/295304/will-the-fenix6-family-ever-be-updated-to-ciq-api-level-4).

2) "System 3/4-era, NOT System 5/6/7" — REFUTED. Two independent pieces of evidence:
 - the5krunner (https://the5krunner.com/2022/03/31/fenix-6-gets-connect-iq-system-5-latest-ciq-update-now-in-beta/) reports fenix 6 firmware 20.82 (beta, 2022) added "Connect IQ system 5" support across all fenix 6 variants (6, 6S, 6 Pro, 6S Pro, 6X Pro) — i.e. fenix 6 is NOT capped at System 3/4.
 - The Garmin developer forum thread "API, CIQ, SDK, SYSTEM #s" (https://forums.garmin.com/developer/connect-iq/f/discussion/402064/api-ciq-sdk-system-s) gives the explicit mapping Garmin uses: each Connect IQ "System" release ships two parallel API tracks, one for legacy CIQ3-class hardware and one for CIQ4+ hardware — e.g. System 5 = API 3.3 (CIQ3 devices) or API 4.1 (CIQ4+ devices); System 6 = API 3.4 (CIQ3 devices) or API 4.2 (CIQ4+ devices). Under this mapping, a device frozen at API 3.4 is the CIQ3-track device for System 6, not "stuck in System 3/4."

So the correct, precise statement is: every fenix 6 variant is permanently capped at Connect IQ **API level 3.4** (the legacy CIQ3 API track) and will never receive API 4.x/5.x — but the devices themselves have been updated via firmware to participate in newer Connect IQ **System** releases (confirmed through System 5, and per Garmin's own System↔API table, API 3.4 corresponds to System 6's CIQ3 track). "API level" and "System version" are not interchangeable, and the claim's parenthetical equating "API 3.4" with being locked out of "System 5/6/7" is not supported by Garmin's own sources — it is refuted.

Practical implication for the Solana-epoch watch face: target Connect IQ API 3.4 (Monkey C, System 3-class runtime: WatchUi, Background/Bluetooth Low Energy or Web Requests API as available at 3.4, no CIQ4-only APIs like Graphics Pools, Complications framework additions past 3.4, etc.) when building for fenix 6/6 Pro/6S/6S Pro/6X Pro and their solar/sapphire/dual-power/tactix/quatix siblings.

Independent corroboration/refutation: https://the5krunner.com/2022/03/31/fenix-6-gets-connect-iq-system-5-latest-ciq-update-now-in-beta/ (fenix 6 series gained Connect IQ System 5 via firmware 20.82); https://forums.garmin.com/outdoor-recreation/outdoor-recreation/f/fenix-6-series/295304/will-the-fenix6-family-ever-be-updated-to-ciq-api-level-4 (Garmin staff confirm fenix 6 permanently capped at API 3.3.x/3.4, hardware lacks CIQ4 "graphics pools"); https://forums.garmin.com/developer/connect-iq/f/discussion/402064/api-ciq-sdk-system-s (explicit System-version-to-API-level mapping table showing System 5/6 both have a CIQ3-track API, i.e. System version and API level are decoupled).

verdict.claim: Average Solana slot time can be computed as samplePeriodSecs / numSlots (or sum(samplePeriodSecs)/sum(numSlots) across samples for smoothing) from getRecentPerformanceSamples; this matches the observed ~190 slots per 60s sample (~0.316 s/slot) on 2026-09-11.
verdict.correction:
The formula itself is correct and the specific figure is independently verifiable — contrary to the claim's framing that it was "not independently re-measured" due to a sandbox timeout. Two corrections to the supporting narrative (the core math claim stands):

1. Primary source (solana.com/docs/rpc/http/getrecentperformancesamples) defines samplePeriodSecs as "the number of seconds in a sample window" and numSlots as "the number of slots completed" during that window, but the doc page itself does NOT explicitly state the samplePeriodSecs/numSlots division formula — that derivation is a reasonable, standard inference from the field semantics, not text lifted from the doc. Third-party docs (e.g. QuickNode's getRecentPerformanceSamples reference) do state this formula explicitly, corroborating the derivation.

2. The claim that outbound curl to api.mainnet-beta.solana.com timed out and the ~0.316s/slot figure was unverified is refuted in this environment: `curl -s -X POST https://api.mainnet-beta.solana.com` with method getRecentPerformanceSamples succeeded just now (2026-09-11) and returned real samples: {numSlots:190, samplePeriodSecs:60} → 60/190 = 0.3158 s/slot, {numSlots:191, samplePeriodSecs:60} → 0.3141 s/slot, {numSlots:186, samplePeriodSecs:60} → 0.3226 s/slot. This independently matches the orchestrator's claimed ~0.316 s/slot almost exactly, and confirms samplePeriodSecs is consistently 60 in current samples (not guaranteed by spec, hence the sum/sum smoothing recommendation in the claim is sound practice, not just a hedge).

Net: the math (formula) is correct and independently corroborated by a secondary source; the specific ~0.316s/slot figure is also independently confirmed live, not merely orchestrator-supplied. Note this measured average (~0.31-0.32s/slot) is notably faster than Solana's commonly cited 400ms target slot time — expected/normal, since numSlots counts slot-height advancement (including any skipped slots) over wall-clock time, and observed network slot rates fluctuate around/below the target depending on cluster conditions; this is a known characteristic, not evidence against the formula.
verdict.evidence:
Primary source: https://solana.com/docs/rpc/http/getrecentperformancesamples (field definitions for samplePeriodSecs, numSlots, numTransactions, numNonVoteTransactions — no explicit division formula stated on the page itself).
Independent corroborating source: QuickNode getRecentPerformanceSamples RPC doc (https://www.quicknode.com/docs/solana/getRecentPerformanceSamples), found via WebSearch, explicitly states "average slot time = samplePeriodSecs / numSlots" with a worked example (126 slots/60s ≈ 476ms).

2) https://developer.garmin.com/connect-iq/api-docs/Toybox/WatchUi/WatchFacePowerInfo.html — CONFIRMED: exposes `executionTimeAverage` ("Average elapsed time per update in milliseconds") and `executionTimeLimit` ("Maximum allowed time in milliseconds"), both `Lang.Float`, and CONFIRMED no numeric default (no "20", no "ms" constant) appears anywhere on the page — it is purely a property reference with no value.

3) https://developer.garmin.com/connect-iq/connect-iq-faq/how-do-i-get-my-watch-face-to-update-every-second/ — REFUTES the claim's own phrasing. I pulled the actual underlying static article (developer.garmin.com/connect-iq/articles/connect-iq-faq/How_Do_I_Get_My_Watch_Face_to_Update_Every_Second.html, reached via the page's Gatsby page-data.json since the FAQ URL itself serves no server-rendered body). If the execution limit is exceeded, the onPowerBudgetExceeded() method will be invoked..." — it never states 20ms, 30ms, or any numeric figure at all. So the claim's assertion that "the 20ms figure comes from Garmin's forum/FAQ summary content" is factually wrong for the FAQ half: the official FAQ page contains no numeric figure whatsoever; only the separate forum announcement post does.

Further, that 20ms figure is not corroborated as a stable documented constant: a Garmin moderator in a separate forum thread cites a different figure ("30ms") for the average allowed onPartialUpdate execution time, and no official Garmin page (API reference or FAQ) states any numeric ms value at all. verdict.claim: getEpochSchedule returns slotsPerEpoch, leaderScheduleSlotOffset, warmup, firstNormalEpoch, firstNormalSlot, and is the authoritative way to confirm epoch length / warmup status per cluster rather than assuming 432000.
verdict.evidence: Primary source (https://solana.com/docs/rpc/http/getepochschedule, fetched live) confirms all five return fields with matching descriptions: slotsPerEpoch (u64, "The maximum number of slots in each epoch"), leaderScheduleSlotOffset (u64, "The number of slots before beginning of an epoch to calculate a leader schedule for that epoch"), warmup (bool, "Whether epochs start short and grow"), firstNormalEpoch (u64, "The first normal-length epoch after the warmup period"), firstNormalSlot (u64, "The first slot in the first normal-length epoch"). Independent source Helius (https://www.helius.dev/docs/api-reference/rpc/http/getepochschedule, fetched live) corroborates the same five fields and semantics (worded slightly differently but substantively identical): warmup = "Boolean indicating if the network uses a warmup period with gradually increasing epoch lengths," firstNormalEpoch = "The first epoch number that reaches full standard length," firstNormalSlot = "the absolute slot number when epochs begin their standard length after the initial warmup period." A supplementary web search confirms the practical point behind the claim: Solana mainnet-beta currently reports slotsPerEpoch=432000, leaderScheduleSlotOffset=432000, warmup=false — i.e., 432000 is a mainnet-beta-specific, warmup-already-completed value, not a protocol-wide constant, which is exactly why the claim's recommendation to call getEpochSchedule per-cluster instead of hardcoding 432000 is correct (devnet/testnet have historically differed and could again). No discrepancy, deprecation notice, or version-specific caveat was found on either source that contradicts the claim. Minor imprecision (not a substantive error): "whether warmup still applies for a given cluster/epoch" slightly overstates per-epoch variability — warmup is a fixed genesis-time flag per cluster/ledger (not something that can flip per individual epoch at runtime), and once an epoch number is ≥ firstNormalEpoch its length is fixed regardless of the warmup flag's original value. This doesn't change the core claim's correctness for the watch face's purpose (query getEpochSchedule once per cluster to derive slot length and warmup status rather than hardcoding 432000).

verdict.claim: Background services are registered via AppBase.getServiceDelegate() as [System.ServiceDelegate]. When triggered, the returned delegate's event method runs, then the process MUST call Background.exit(data) or System.exit(); if it doesn't, the OS force-terminates it after 30 seconds.
verdict.evidence:
Primary source, developer.garmin.com/connect-iq/api-docs/Toybox/Application/AppBase.html#getServiceDelegate-instance_function (fetched directly, full entry quoted): "Get a ServiceDelegate to run background tasks for this app. ... When a ServiceDelegate is retrieved, the following will occur: The method triggered within the ServiceDelegate will be run. The background task will exit using Background.exit() or System.exit(). The background task will be automatically terminated after 30 seconds if it is not exited by these methods." Return type is documented as `[ System.ServiceDelegate ]` (array), matching the claim's bracket notation exactly.

Corroborating primary source, developer.garmin.com/connect-iq/articles/core-topics/Backgrounding.html: "When background services are started, the AppBase.getServiceDelegate() is called... This method returns a System.ServiceDelegate... Once a background service has finished any necessary tasks, it should exit using the Background.exit() method. This method takes a[n] argument containing data to be sent to the main process... Services will also be terminated automatically if they do not exit properly within 30 seconds of opening." — confirms Background.exit(data) signature and the 30s ceiling. (Available since API level 2.3.0, so API 3.x on fenix 6 is covered.)

Independent source, Garmin forum (forums.garmin.com/developer/connect-iq/f/discussion/330437/background-process-termination), Garmin employee jim_m_58: "A background service runs for at most 30 seconds at a time," consistent with the 30-second force-termination window.

The "event method" wording matches Toybox.System.ServiceDelegate's documented callbacks (onTemporalEvent, onPhoneAppMessage, onOAuthResponse, etc., per developer.garmin.com/connect-iq/api-docs/Toybox/System/ServiceDelegate.html) — i.e. "the returned delegate's event method" is the specific callback (e.g. onTemporalEvent) that getServiceDelegate's caller wires up, not a generic single method name.

Caveat (does not refute the documentation, but is a real-world discrepancy worth flagging for the fenix 6 build): multiple Garmin forum threads (e.g. forums.garmin.com/developer/connect-iq/i/bug-reports/background-service-failing-for-some-people and the same discussion thread above) report that on some fenix devices the background service is observed to terminate well before the documented 30 seconds (one report: ~1 second), so the JSON-RPC HTTP request to Solana RPC may not reliably complete in the background slot on fenix 6 hardware in practice — plan for this with retries/caching rather than assuming a full 30s window is usable.

verdict.claim: Data delivered via exit() reaches AppBase.onBackgroundData(data) — called immediately if the foreground app is active, otherwise cached and delivered right after the app's onStart() runs on next launch. AppBase.getBackgroundData() can also pull it and resets to null once consumed.
verdict.correction: The onBackgroundData timing description is correct and confirmed at the cited URL: AppBase.onBackgroundData(data as Application.PersistableType) as Void is called immediately if the main app is active, otherwise the payload is cached and delivered right after onStart() completes on next launch. However, getBackgroundData() is NOT a method on Toybox.Application.AppBase — it does not appear anywhere on the cited AppBase.html doc page. It is instead a method of the separate Toybox.Background module (Background.getBackgroundData(), documented at developer.garmin.com/connect-iq/api-docs/Toybox/Background.html). Its real purpose is to be called from inside the background delegate to see what data is currently queued-but-undelivered to the main process (so it can be merged with new results before the next Background.exit()); when called from the main/foreground process it always returns null. The 'resets to null once consumed' detail is real but applies to the queued background-side data, not to something AppBase exposes.
verdict.evidence: Primary source (fetched directly): https://developer.garmin.com/connect-iq/api-docs/Toybox/Application/AppBase.html — contains onBackgroundData(data as Application.PersistableType) as Void with description "If the main application is active when this occurs, the data will be passed directly to the application's onBackgroundData() method. If the main application is not active, the data will be saved until the next time the application is launched and will be passed to the application after the onStart() method completes." No getBackgroundData entry exists on this page. Independent confirmation of the module split: https://developer.garmin.com/connect-iq/api-docs/Toybox/Background.html lists getBackgroundData() → Application.PropertyValueType as a Toybox.Background module method ("Retrieves data previously saved by a background process... Returns null in the main application process... Data is reset to null once delivered to main process"), and Garmin forum discussion at https://forums.garmin.com/developer/connect-iq/f/discussion/408604/onbackgrounddata-not-called-from-when-background-exit-is-called-from-makewebrequest-callback corroborates real-world usage of Background.getBackgroundData() from within the background delegate to combine queued-but-undelivered data with new results before exit().</evidence>

verdict.claim: slotsInEpoch is NOT hard-coded/documented as always 432000 by the getEpochInfo docs page itself (example shows 8192); 432,000 is DEFAULT_SLOTS_PER_EPOCH used on mainnet-beta post-warmup, so in practice slotsInEpoch == 432000 on mainnet-beta today.
verdict.correction: The doc-page-text portion is accurate and confirmed by direct fetch: solana.com/docs/rpc/http/getEpochInfo describes slotsInEpoch generically and its example response literally shows slotsInEpoch:8192, with no 432000 mentioned anywhere on the page. The existence of the 432,000 constant is also confirmed, and from a stronger primary source than the one cited: Solana core source (github.com/solana-labs/solana/blob/master/sdk/program/src/clock.rs) defines `pub const DEFAULT_SLOTS_PER_EPOCH: u64 = 2 * TICKS_PER_DAY / DEFAULT_TICKS_PER_SLOT;` = 432,000, comment "1 Epoch ~= 2 days" — this is a better source than the solanavalidators.wiki page cited in the claim, which I also fetched and confirmed says "A Solana epoch is a fixed window of 432,000 slots." However, the claim's final empirical leg — 'in practice slotsInEpoch == 432000 on mainnet-beta today' — was NOT verified in this check: I did not make a live JSON-RPC call to mainnet-beta's getEpochInfo/getEpochSchedule to confirm the current runtime value. DEFAULT_SLOTS_PER_EPOCH is a client default baked into genesis-config generation, not a value the docs or the constant itself guarantee is what any given live cluster (including mainnet-beta) is actually running post-warmup — the genesis config could in principle set a different slotsPerEpoch. For a watch face implementation, do not hard-code 432000 from this constant alone; call getEpochInfo (for slotsInEpoch, absoluteSlot, slotIndex) and/or getEpochSchedule live against your mainnet-beta RPC endpoint at runtime/build-time to confirm the actual current value rather than trusting the DEFAULT_SLOTS_PER_EPOCH-implies-live-value inference.
verdict.evidence: Fetched https://solana.com/docs/rpc/http/getEpochInfo directly: slotsInEpoch documented only as 'Total number of slots in the current epoch'; example JSON shows "slotsInEpoch": 8192; no numeric constant or 432000 stated on the page. Fetched https://solana.com/docs/rpc/http/getEpochSchedule directly: slotsPerEpoch/firstNormalEpoch/warmup fields documented as described; no 432000 text on that page either. Fetched https://github.com/solana-labs/solana/blob/master/sdk/program/src/clock.rs directly: confirms `DEFAULT_SLOTS_PER_EPOCH: u64 = 2 * TICKS_PER_DAY / DEFAULT_TICKS_PER_SLOT` = 432,000, comment '1 Epoch ~= 2 days' — a primary/authoritative independent source, stronger than the wiki cited in the claim. Fetched https://solanavalidators.wiki/glossary/epoch/ directly: confirmed exact quoted text 'A Solana epoch is a fixed window of 432,000 slots — approximately 2 days of actual wall-clock time on the current network.' No live RPC call was made to mainnet-beta's getEpochInfo/getEpochSchedule endpoints in this check, so the 'today, in practice' runtime assertion remains unconfirmed by direct evidence gathered here.

verdict.claim: onEnterSleep() means "the device is entering low power mode" — terminate active timers and prepare for once-per-minute updates. onExitSleep() means "the device is exiting low power mode" — timers/animations may be started here, in preparation for once-per-second updates. Both are API level 1.0.0.
verdict.evidence:
Primary source (developer.garmin.com/connect-iq/api-docs/Toybox/WatchUi/WatchFace.html, fetched live) gives the exact wording:
- onEnterSleep() as Void — "Since: API Level 1.0.0" — "The device is entering low power mode. Terminate any active timers and prepare for once-per-minute updates."
- onExitSleep() as Void — "Since: API Level 1.0.0" — "The device is exiting low power mode. Timers and animations may be started here in preparation for once-per-second updates."
This is a verbatim match to the claim, including both methods being pinned at API level 1.0.0 (the base Connect IQ API level, so it applies unchanged on fenix 6 / CIQ 3.x — no version-specific divergence in the definition or API level).

Independent corroboration from an official Garmin forum thread (forums.garmin.com/developer/connect-iq/f/discussion/6170/onexitsleep-not-triggered) confirms the same semantics from a different angle: with Low Power Mode enabled, onUpdate() is called once per minute (the onEnterSleep state); with it disabled, onUpdate() runs every second and onEnterSleep()/onExitSleep() fire on the transitions — consistent with the doc's "once-per-minute" / "once-per-second" framing. A contributor also confirms onExitSleep() is triggered by the wrist "look at watch" gesture and onEnterSleep() fires ~10s after entering sleep.

Caveat (does not refute the claim, but matters for your fenix 6 implementation): the same forum thread documents a known firmware-level bug on some devices/firmware where onExitSleep() fails to fire reliably (gesture recognition tied to backlight behavior in low-power mode), so a watch face should not assume onExitSleep() is guaranteed to run every wrist-raise on real hardware — design your epoch-countdown redraw logic to tolerate a missed onExitSleep() (e.g., always recompute from onUpdate()'s current time rather than relying on state set only in onExitSleep()). No fenix 6-specific or CIQ 3.x-specific override of the 1.0.0 API-level definition was found.

verdict.claim: Background.exit(backgroundData) accepts String, Number, Float, Boolean, Char, Long, Double, Array, or Dictionary (nested Array/Dictionary allowed, null values allowed). Data size limit is 'approximately 8 KB'; exceeding it throws Background.ExitDataSizeLimitException and the process does NOT exit (must retry exit() with less data). exit() is a no-op if called from the foreground app process.
verdict.evidence:
Primary source fetched directly: https://developer.garmin.com/connect-iq/api-docs/Toybox/Background.html — exit() takes an Application.PropertyValueType parameter, whose accepted types are exactly String, Number, Float, Boolean, Char, Long, Double, plus Array and Dictionary (which may nest and may contain null). The page's own wording: "This method will exit if called by a background process, but will do nothing if called by the main application process" — confirming the foreground no-op behavior verbatim. ExitDataSizeLimitException's documented description: "the data provided exceeds the data size limit (approximately 8 KB)"; on catching it the background process remains alive (has not exited) and the documented remedy is to reduce data size and call Background.exit() again — matching the "process does NOT exit, must retry with less data" claim exactly.

Independent corroboration: Garmin developer forum thread https://forums.garmin.com/developer/connect-iq/f/discussion/7550/data-too-large-for-background-process discusses hitting this same ~8KB ExitDataSizeLimitException limit in practice, confirms the limit is approximate (serialization overhead counts against it, so usable space can be less than 8KB), and confirms the standard remedy is trimming the payload and retrying exit() with less data.

One secondary attempt to cross-check against the older SDK-bundled mirror (https://developer.garmin.com/downloads/connect-iq/monkey-c/doc/Toybox/Background.html) 404'd, but this doesn't undermine the claim since the current, authoritative developer.garmin.com/connect-iq/api-docs page (the claimed source) was fetched successfully and its content matches the claim point-for-point, with independent forum confirmation of the practical behavior (approximate limit, overhead counts, retry-with-less-data remedy). No version-specific contradiction was found for API 3.x/fenix 6 — Background.exit() and ExitDataSizeLimitException predate Connect IQ 3.x (Background module has existed since early Connect IQ 2.x releases) so this API surface applies unchanged to a fenix 6 (API 3.x) watch face. I could not find any documented contradiction, deprecation, or version-gated change to these specific semantics.

verdict.claim: Graphics font constants are relative sizes, not fixed pixel values: FONT_XTINY=0 ... FONT_NUMBER_HOT=7, FONT_NUMBER_THAI_HOT=8, with value 6 "undocumented ... possibly a deprecated/internal id"; per-device pixel heights aren't published; Garmin guidance is to measure at runtime via getFontAscent()/getFontDescent()/getTextDimensions() or consult "Appendix B" of the CIQ UX guide.
verdict.evidence: Primary source fetched directly: https://developer.garmin.com/connect-iq/api-docs/Toybox/Graphics.html — lists 29 FONT_* constants including FONT_NUMBER_MEDIUM=6 (public, documented, sits between FONT_NUMBER_MILD=5 and FONT_NUMBER_HOT=7), and documents getFontAscent(), getFontDescent(), getFontHeight() as the recommended runtime sizing methods; no per-device pixel table is present on the page. Independent corroboration via WebSearch: an official Garmin layout-XML example uses font="Graphics.FONT_NUMBER_MEDIUM", confirming it is a live, public, non-deprecated constant, not an internal/undocumented id. Forum sources fetched: https://forums.garmin.com/developer/connect-iq/f/discussion/348347/device-info-glance-yes-no-and-size-and-font-size-width-in-pixel (guidance is dc.getTextWidthInPixels(), no per-device pixel table given; the "px number in device ref" question is left unanswered) and https://forums.garmin.com/developer/connect-iq/f/discussion/5148/font-heights (confirms getFontHeight() returns pixels but with device-varying padding, e.g. Fenix 3 HR FONT_NUMBER_MEDIUM reports 60px vs ~40px visible glyph height; this thread does NOT mention getFontAscent(), getFontDescent(), getTextDimensions(), or "Appendix B" at all).
verdict.correction:
The "relative sizes, measure at runtime" thesis is directionally correct and confirmed by both forum threads. But the claim is wrong on value 6: FONT_NUMBER_MEDIUM=6 is a fully public, actively-documented Connect IQ constant (confirmed both on the official API page and via an independent official layout-XML usage example) — it is not "undocumented" and there is no basis to call it "possibly a deprecated/internal id." Also, the claim's cited runtime API "getTextDimensions()" is not the method actually documented on the Graphics page for this purpose — the documented trio is getFontAscent(), getFontDescent(), and getFontHeight() (ascent+descent); getTextDimensions was not found there. Additionally, forum thread 5148 does not reference getFontAscent/getFontDescent/getTextDimensions at all, so the claim overstates that thread's alignment with the "measure via these methods" advice. Neither forum thread mentions an "Appendix B" of a UX guide — this part is unverifiable (not confirmed, not contradicted) rather than supporting evidence, and the claim's own hedge acknowledges it wasn't located.</parameter>
</invoke>

verdict.claim: getEpochInfo returns {absoluteSlot, blockHeight, epoch, slotIndex, slotsInEpoch, transactionCount} (transactionCount is u64|null), with the six field descriptions as quoted, per https://solana.com/docs/rpc/http/getEpochInfo.

- "Slot index within the current epoch." (slotIndex, !type u64)

This is stronger evidence than the WebFetch tool's paraphrased summaries (which returned this same wording twice independently, corroborating it) — the raw curl removes any risk of small-model paraphrase/hallucination on the primary source.

Third-party mirrors (QuickNode, Chainstack) also use their own independently-written short phrasing, not the claim's wording — but those are not the cited source and were only checked as corroboration attempts. Since the claim explicitly cites the solana.com URL and that page's actual content matches the claim's quotes verbatim, the claim stands confirmed as written; the GitHub-mismatch is a noteworthy footnote about docs-source staleness, not a refutation of the claim itself. Field types (u64, and u64|null for transactionCount) are also confirmed correct and unchanged.
